chapter_title: Chương 287: 0288【Game offline cũng kiếm được tiền?】

segments.title: Chương 287: 0288【Game offline cũng kiếm được tiền?】
segments.content:
China actually has a large number of single-player gamers.

But they either buy pirated installation discs or download pirated installation packages online.

Because the official retail price for domestic single-player games is basically set at 38 yuan.

From this 38 yuan price, after deducting the cuts for distributors and publishers, and then deducting various production, warehousing, and logistics costs, the game developer only makes 4 yuan per disc. And that's 4 yuan before tax.

The distributors make the lion's share, taking a direct 50% cut!

Looking at it this way, it's very reasonable for Chen Guiliang to sell it for 5 yuan a copy on his own platform.

Other single-player game companies could do the same.

Because the Youke platform only takes a 20% cut, if a developer sells a game for 5 yuan a copy on the Youke platform, they can still earn 4 yuan per copy. It's about the same as what they make selling a 38 yuan installation disc.

On the last day of 2006, Chen Guiliang posted a message simultaneously on his Xiaonei and Hainei accounts:

"Although *Plants vs. Zombies* can be played online, it is, at its core, a single-player game. This game was in development for 5 months, with a team of 6 and some outsourcing, and the total development cost was 1 million yuan. If we sell it for 5 yuan a copy, even without counting other costs (like taxes), we need to sell 200,000 copies to break even."

"As everyone knows, it's very difficult to sell 200,000 official copies in China. So this game is destined to lose money. The company can't be bothered to promote it. The more we invest in promotion, the more we'll lose."

"I'm just promoting it a little on my personal social accounts. Those who like single-player games can go pay to download and play it."

"I only ask the brothers who make cracked versions to please upload the pirated resources three months later, to give the official version some room to break even. If you drive all the official versions to extinction, you'll only be able to crack foreign games in the future."

"My sincere thanks!"

The message was posted, and the reaction was strong.

A large number of Chen Guiliang's fans, as well as single-player game enthusiasts, spontaneously reposted the article to Tieba and forums.

The WoW Ba at this time was full of World of Warcraft players; there wasn't a large number of non-gaming members yet. When this message was reposted there, the replies reached several thousand in a single day.

"Honestly, after reading what Mr. Chen wrote, I feel very sad. The domestic single-player scene used to be so prosperous, all ruined by piracy. Kingsoft, Target, Pixel, Softstar, Heluo, T-Time, Firestone... so many single-player developers have either gone bankrupt or switched to making online games. Those who can still stick to single-player games are few and far between, and all of them are struggling to survive."

"Haha, I am guilty. I've never spent money on single-player games."

"What kind of game can you make in 5 months for 1 million yuan? It's definitely garbage."

"Garbage my ass! These days, you're guaranteed to lose money making a single-player game for 1 million. It's a deal that's certain to lose money, and it's already a rare thing that someone is willing to do it."

"Sigh, I'll support it. 5 yuan isn't even enough to buy two bottles of Coke. I spend tens of yuan on my WoW game time card every month."

"Some people, they'll top up tens of yuan for game time cards without a second thought, but they think a 5 yuan single-player game is too expensive."

"Brothers who have pre-ordered, come back and tell us about the game after you've played it. I'm waiting online for a report. If it's good, I'll buy it."

"Damn it, you're waiting for a report for 5 yuan. How broke are you?"

"This has nothing to do with being broke. I'm naturally willing to spend money on fun games. For games that aren't fun, I'd find it too expensive even if it was 1 yuan."

"Are you sure it's the official version? The pirated game discs I bought in middle school were 10 yuan."

"Let's go, let's go, the pre-order army is on the move."

"It seems like the download will be available after 12 AM tonight. I'm not going to run dungeons tonight, I'll download the single-player game first and check it out."

Tao Weize was a loyal *World of Warcraft* player.

But he was even more of a veteran gamer.

He played the Famicom and handhelds in elementary school, started playing arcade games in middle school, got into PC single-player games in high school, and only started playing online games in college.

His family wasn't wealthy, but they couldn't be called poor either.

Just an ordinary family from a small city.

"Huh, Old Tao, why are you logging off so early tonight?" his roommate Hong Gang asked in surprise.

Tao Weize said, "I didn't enter a dungeon. Once you start, it takes one or two hours."

Another roommate, who was chatting online, said with a laugh, "The final exams are still more than half a month away. You're not going to quit gaming to prepare for review, are you?"

Tao Weize smiled and said nothing.

Suddenly, the dormitory lights went out, and the campus network was disconnected.

But the power sockets still had electricity, and the personal broadband connections were still on, so students playing on their computers were not affected.

Tao Weize switched back and forth between Xiaonei and WoW Ba, browsing various blog posts and threads. After 12 AM, he clicked to download *Plants vs. Zombies*.

He left it downloading and went back to replying to posts.

He thought it would take a long time to download, but surprisingly, he heard a "ding" after just over 40 minutes. He thought his roommate's porn had finished downloading.

"Damn, such a small game? Don't tell me I've been scammed!" Tao Weize muttered to himself.

The installation package for the original version of *Plants vs. Zombies* was only about 60 MB, and the game size after installation was just over 90 MB. Very crude!

But Chen Guiliang's version was made to be a bit more polished, and it had more levels. After installation, it was 220 MB. If you were online, you could also see your ranking.

Once the installation was complete, Tao Weize logged in directly with his Youke account.

The game screen showed an opening narration: "In a quiet little town, lived a farmer. One day, while the farmer was munching on a cob of corn, he suddenly discovered zombies popping up in your yard. He rushed into your house in a panic, wearing a pot on his head as a helmet, and shouted: Bro, the zombies are here, we have to plant some plants!"

Next was the new player tutorial.

The farmer said to you: "Look, the zombies are shambling over from the road! Quick, plant sunflowers in the yard, they can produce sun."

Sunflowers can produce sun?

Sun can kill zombies?

Tao Weize found it both funny and interesting, and followed the tutorial to plant a sunflower.

Then he followed the tutorial to plant a pea, and after watching the peashooter spit the first zombie to death, Tao Weize thought, this game is so damn ridiculous. Which clever little rascal came up with this bizarre setting?

As the tutorial ended, a game subtitle prompted: "You are about to enter Adventure Mode. After clearing Adventure Mode, you can unlock Survival Mode (Normal). There are also hidden levels waiting for you to unlock."

Adventure Mode was quite simple, but that was relative to experienced players.

Tao Weize had never played a tower defense game before, and by the time he reached level 30-something, he started to struggle a bit, but he still managed to clear all 50 levels without any real danger.

"The first chapter of Adventure Mode is complete. Congratulations on clearing it. The second chapter of Adventure Mode is currently under development. You can now go challenge the first chapter of Survival Mode (Normal)."

Tao Weize said, "Damn, this game actually has future updates? They've only finished the first chapter."

Tao Weize started playing Survival Mode (Normal). The map was largely similar to Adventure Mode, but there were some subtle changes. In particular, the zombies' speed had increased, and their health bars had become thicker.

"Damn it!" Tao Weize slammed his keyboard. This time, he was done for after only seven levels.

The game screen even displayed a subtitle: "Your brains were eaten by the zombies..."

All of his roommates were night owls. Since it was the New Year's Day holiday and there were no classes, none of them were asleep yet.

Hearing the commotion from Tao Weize, they all looked over curiously.

They saw him playing Survival Mode again, planting all sorts of plants to fight the zombies.

"Whoa, what game is this? The art style is so weird."

"Take off your headphones, play it through the speakers."

"Is that a pea?"

"Old Tao, where did you download this game?"

"What download? Just have Old Tao copy it over."

Tao Weize said, "You have to buy this game. Copying it won't work, there's a genuine verification code. If you want to play a free cracked version, you'll have to wait."

Upon hearing that they had to pay for a genuine copy, the others all started to back down.

Tao Weize added, "It only costs 5 yuan, it's very cheap."

"5 yuan is still money. I'll wait for the pirated version."

"Exactly, who plays the official version when there's a pirated one? We'll talk about it when the pirated version comes out."

His roommates all said they wouldn't buy it.

Tao Weize was a bit annoyed to hear this. "Old Zhou, you often take girls out to eat. You treat this one today, that one tomorrow. Which meal doesn't cost tens of yuan? You think a 5 yuan official game is too expensive?"

The roommate argued, "Of course I have to spend money to treat a girl to a meal. You don't necessarily have to spend money to play a game."

Several roommates gathered around.

Tao Weize said, "Chen Guiliang is making this game at a loss. He knows he'll lose money but he's still willing to do it. This is love for single-player games, we can't break his heart. If the sales are particularly bad, he won't make them anymore in the future, and there will definitely be no future updates."

One roommate looked at the article and said, "What do I care if he's losing money or not? He's got plenty of it anyway."

Another roommate said, "When I start working and have an income, I'll definitely support him. Right now I'm a poor student, and he's a big boss. He should be the one supporting me."

A third roommate said, "Making a game at a loss? Who is he kidding? He's definitely making the money back from somewhere!"

The remaining two roommates quietly went to pay for and download the official version.

There were six people in the whole dorm, and for half of them to be willing to pay was already a very high ratio.

Of course, the main reason was the cheap price. 5 yuan was really nothing.

If the price had been set at 38 yuan, probably even Tao Weize would not have been willing to buy it.

The next day, during the daytime.

On major Tieba and forums, many players posted threads, sharing their enjoyment of the game with text and screenshots.

Someone even registered a "Plants vs. Zombies Ba."

17173 didn't have a section for *Plants vs. Zombies*, because opening one cost money.

A premium online game section was 500,000 a month.

Even a new online game testing section was 50,000 to 80,000 a month.

The single-player section was more modest, with 3 editors responsible for over a hundred single-player game sections. They simply couldn't keep up.

A new single-player game section was 10,000 to 30,000 a month.

Classic old single-player game sections were free.

Sections for uncommercialized indie games were free, but you had to sign a revenue-sharing agreement with 17173.

As the number of *Plants vs. Zombies* players grew, they began to post in the sections for classic old single-player games.

Would promoting *Plants vs. Zombies* in the section for *The Legend of Sword and Fairy* cause dissatisfaction among Sword and Fairy players?

It wouldn't!

In fact, the atmosphere was particularly harmonious, with a "wish you a good life" kind of beauty to it.

Because single-player game fans all knew that the number of companies willing to make single-player games was dwindling and on the verge of extinction. No matter what kind of game it was, even if it was an H-rated mini-game, everyone was willing to support it.

In just a few days, word-of-mouth promotional posts for *Plants vs. Zombies* took over the major classic old single-player sections on 17173.

It got to the point where 17173 took the initiative to contact Game Science: "You guys should open a new single-player game section. It doesn't cost much, to prevent players from not being able to find a home... What? You don't want to increase costs? I have the authority to give you the lowest price, 10,000 yuan a month... Okay, okay, I'll go apply for another discount."

17173 was also helpless. The single-player section hadn't had a new release for a long time and had been operating at a loss. That's why they had no choice but to cut the number of editors to 3.

Two days later, the 17173 section for *Plants vs. Zombies* was finally opened. It was as cheap as 3,000 yuan a month.

But the popularity of the section was extremely high!

"How many did you say?" Chen Guiliang asked in surprise.

"83,000 copies. In less than 10 days, *Plants vs. Zombies* sold 83,000 copies!"

"Damn, at this rate, we can break even."

"It's probably because it's cheap. It's only 5 yuan, so a lot of people just bought it on a whim."

In the past few years, the best-selling game was *Sword and Fairy 3* (300,000 copies), followed by *Xuan-Yuan Sword 4* (150,000 copies).

But in the last year or two, the single-player market was pretty much dead. The best-selling *Prince of Qin* only sold 80,000 copies.

In less than 10 days, *Plants vs. Zombies* had already surpassed the sales of *Prince of Qin*.

Chen Guiliang posted an article on his personal account again, and it was only one sentence: "This broken game might actually break even? Are you guys forcing me to release an update quickly? Or are you forcing me to continue making single-player games?"

Although *Plants vs. Zombies* had not yet broken even, and even if it did, it wouldn't make much money.

But it had attracted great attention within the industry.

A large number of well-known game developers, who had been forced to switch to making online games, now actively recommended *Plants vs. Zombies*, like mothers who had lost their own children and would cuddle someone else's cute child for a bit.

Many game producers even came to register accounts on Hainei to interact with Chen Guiliang's account.

The three remaining single-player game editors at 17173 praised it to the high heavens, coming up with all sorts of ways to hype *Plants vs. Zombies* up. Because besides this game, there were no other single-player games for them to hype.

And then, the cracked version came out.

In just over twenty days, *Plants vs. Zombies* had a cracked version.

Chen Guiliang was so depressed that he posted again: "No, but it's only been a few days? Big brothers who make cracked versions, can't you be a little more merciful? I haven't even broken even yet, you really have to crush me with one blow, don't you?"

Many netizens went to download the pirated version.

But many other netizens hurled abuse at those who released the pirated resources. In their own words: "Playing a pirated version of a 5 yuan game, this is just dirt-poor crazy. Making a pirated version in just over 20 days, can't even wait a month, those people who crack games are all bastards!"

This time it was really too much.

A company was finally willing to make a single-player game, and the initial sales were pretty good, but a pirated version came out in just over 20 days.

Numerous offline and online media outlets, including *Popular Software* and 17173, collectively condemned the crackers and called on players to buy the official game.

It quickly sparked a heated discussion.

Inexplicably, the sales of *Plants vs. Zombies* broke through 300,000 copies.

Not only did it break even, it even made a small profit.

Chen Guiliang posted for the fourth time, typing only a string of ellipses: "..."

The players of the official version, however, celebrated wildly under this post, as if they were celebrating a great victory.
